introduction: Cass ran the Public Farm floor for nine seasons, and every season someone answered him by talking about his voice or his comb instead of his point. He has a name for that trick. He also has a way of teaching it, and you will not like the way.
introductionSummary: Cass names a trick he has been on the receiving end of for nine seasons, then uses it on you so you will hear it coming.

logicalFallacies.explanation: Attacking the animal instead of the argument. Whether Rue is a raccoon who arrived in a mud cart has nothing to do with the water.

sentences.text: Nine seasons I ran the Public Farm floor. Nine.
Every season, someone answered me by talking about my voice, or my comb, or how I look when I moult.
Never about the motion. Never once about what I had actually said.

statement.summary: Cass has spent nine seasons being answered by remarks about his voice and his comb instead of his point.

sentences.text: There is a name for that trick.
A common misuse of speaking — so common the animals doing it rarely notice they are doing it.
I learned it the long way, by being the thing they pointed at.

statement.summary: Cass says the trick has a name, and that he learned it by being its target.

sentences.text: I can give you the name and sit down.
Or I can show you, which is how anyone actually learns it.
Well?

opponentPrompt.summary: Cass offers the name as a word, or a demonstration, and waits.

options.reason: You answered an offer to teach with an attack on the teacher. That is the trick. You just used it.
options.summary: You dismiss Cass as a cranky old rooster nobody listens to, and so use the trick on the animal offering to name it.

sentences.text: You only know about it because you're a cranky old rooster nobody listens to.

logicalFallacies.explanation: Whether Cass is cranky, old, or ignored has nothing to do with whether the trick has a name. You attacked the teacher instead of taking the lesson.

options.reason: A name without the thing is a word. You will forget it by Sunday.
options.summary: You ask for the name and skip the demonstration.

sentences.text: Just tell me the name.

options.reason: You asked to see it. That is the only way the name will stick.
options.summary: You ask him to show you, which is the lesson he wanted.

sentences.text: Show me.
That's it. You just did it to me. Now watch me do it to you.

statement.summary: Cass names what you just did, then turns the demonstration on you.

sentences.text: A word without the thing is a word. Watch first.

statement.summary: Cass refuses to hand over a name without showing the trick.

sentences.text: Good. Watch.

statement.summary: Cass approves, and the demonstration begins.

sentences.text: Right. I'll be Duchess.
Nobody's blaming you, dear. It's simply that a raccoon who arrived in a mud cart, straw still in his ears, can hardly be expected to know about water.

logicalFallacies.explanation: The claim on the floor is about the water. This sentence answers it by describing Rue — raccoon, mud cart, straw — which tells us nothing about the pond.

sentences.text: The Flock waters at the pond every morning, as they always have.

statement.summary: Cass plays Duchess: a gentle line about the mud cart and the straw, dressed as concern, instead of a line about the water.

sentences.text: That is the whole trick.
She talked about what you are — a raccoon, a mud cart, six weeks — and never about what happened to the water.
The phrase to keep is this: what I am, against what happened. If a line is about you instead of the pond, you have heard it. The name is Ad Hominem.

statement.summary: Cass names the trick Ad Hominem and hands you the phrase: what I am, against what happened.

steps.message:
Cass is going to tell you something.

**[muted]No score here.[/muted]**
Cass just used it on you. Open the **[accent]magnifying glass[/accent]** and read his line sentence by sentence.
Pick the sentence that talks about **[accent]you[/accent]** instead of the water, tag it **[accent]Ad Hominem[/accent]**, submit.
